lesson.title: V→B Word Hunt
lesson.subtitle: Atlas-bridged derivation drills across the whole quiet family

hook.title: The Hunt
hook.content: The Atlas bridge card for this family lists every v→b word in the compendium — today you hunt them all. The verbs: geben, leben, lieben, glauben. The numbers and measures: sieben, halb. The preposition: über. The materials and creatures: Silber/silver, gelb/yellow, Kalb/calf, Leber/liver, Laub/leaf, Rabe/raven. Thirteen words, one law: English v/f between vowels, German b. The hunt's trick is direction — you can run it German→English (Silber → silver?) or English→German (heaven → Himmel is no pair — different family; only true v→b words answer).

footnotes.title: The Raven's Test
footnotes.content: Rabe ↔ raven is the cleanest proof of the law: an ordinary bird, an ordinary word, and the v/b correspondence perfectly preserved. When a law works on ravens, rivers, and livers, it is a law.

pattern.title: The Hunt Grid
pattern.content: Grid one — verbs: give/geben, live/leben, love/lieben, believe/glauben (be↔ge + lieve/laube). Grid two — quantity: seven/sieben, half/halb. Grid three — position: over/über. Grid four — materials: silver/Silber, yellow/gelb (double shift — y→g too!). Grid five — bodies and beasts: calf/Kalb, liver/Leber, leaf/Laub, raven/Rabe, beaver/Biber. Each grid is a derivation drill: cover the German, produce it from the English by shifting the consonant, then check. This family is the Atlas's quietest constellation — and one of its most reliable.
pattern.linguist_note: gelb/yellow is the family's showcase: TWO shifts at once (y→g and v/f→b) on one color word. Proto-Germanic *gelwaz carried both — English vocalized the g, softened the w; German kept the g, closed the w. One word, two evolutionary reports.

exercises.prompt: Hunt grid — match the bodies and beasts:
exercises.target_answer: das Kalb, die Leber, das Laub, der Rabe, selbst
exercises.explanation: Unrelated meanings, one law: the English v/f closes to German b between vowels — and selbst is the law living in your own pronouns.

exercises.prompt: The showcase: 'gelb' (yellow) carries TWO shifts. Which?
exercises.explanation: The g of gelb is the y English vocalized; the b is the w English softened. One color, two reports. And while you hunt: predicate adjectives stay bare — der Kuchen ist lecker, alles ist neu, der Kühlschrank ist voll, die Straße ist nass — endings belong to attributives, not predicates.
be- ↔ ge- and lieve → laube (v→b): both elements correspond. The prefix pairs ride together.

exercises.prompt: What English metal is the twin of 'Silber'?
exercises.explanation: The v closed to b — and silver/gelb shows the family covers materials as happily as verbs.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'We believe, we live, we love' (the verbs' anthem)
exercises.target_answer: Wir glauben wir leben wir lieben
exercises.meaning: We believe, we live, we love
exercises.explanation: Three quiet-family verbs in one rhythm — the V→B family is where German keeps its heart-words.

summary.outcome: Derive the whole V→B family in both directions across five word grids.

use_example.german: Wir glauben, wir leben, wir lieben.
use_example.english: We believe, we live, we love.

summary.takeaway: English v/f between vowels → German b: thirteen words from verbs to ravens, one law end to end.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: Hidden Shifts II — gh→ch and y→g: the ghost-letter map, from Nacht/night to sagen/say.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from V→B Word Hunt (We believe, we live, we love):
twist.target_answer: Wir glauben wir leben wir lieben
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Wir glauben wir leben wir lieben" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of V→B Word Hunt without relying on short-term echo.

geben.context_translation: There is a problem (literally: it gives a problem).
geben.etymology_derivation: v → b. In impersonal form "es gibt", expresses existence.

glauben.etymology_derivation: be- ↔ ge- & lieve ↔ lauben (v → b). Governs dative case.

über.context_translation: We are speaking about / over the book.

halb.context_translation: It is half past seven (halfway to eight).

silber.context_translation: The ring is made of silver.

gelb.etymology_derivation: Double shift: y → g and w/v → b (yellow → gelb).

kalb.context_phrase: Die Kuh hat ein kleines Kalb.
kalb.context_translation: The cow has a small calf.

laub.context_phrase: Das bunte Laub fällt von den Bäumen.
laub.context_translation: The colorful foliage falls from the trees.

selbst.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *selbaz; the page lists English self as the direct cognate — the f closing to b in German plus an excrescent t. [wiktionary]

lecker.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German lecker, tied to the verb lecken, to lick, Proto-West Germanic *likkōn; the entry points to English lick as the relative, so the word family is literally about licking. [wiktionary]

neu.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German niuwe, Proto-Germanic *niwjaz, the exact twin of English new; both go back to the same Indo-European root. [wiktionary]

voll.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *fullaz — English full is the explicit cognate. [wiktionary]

nass.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *nat — cognate with Dutch nat; English wet is a translation match, not a cognate. [wiktionary]

herbst.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *harbist — English harvest is the twin, with English v ↔ German b. [wiktionary]

überall.context_translation: I am looking everywhere for my glasses.
überall.etymology_derivation: Über (twin of English over — English v became German b) plus all (twin of all); the page itself says compare English overall. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
